**Non-planar 3D Printing Based on Coral Reef Morphology (Sample)** Wenjun Liu, Xingxin He

**1. Introduction**

**Concept &amp; Goals:**

We propose to fabricate a bio-inspired artificial reef structure using robotic non-planar 3D printing  technology. The primary purpose of the installation is to support coral population restoration by providing  a suitable substrate for coral larval attachment and growth. The design incorporates highly organic forms,  continuously varying curvatures, and complex porous structures that mimic natural reef ecosystems.

This project aims to explore the formal and functional possibilities of non-planar 3D printing while  addressing urgent ecological challenges through design innovation.

Our main goals include:

1. Exploring segmentation algorithms for complex surfaces to ensure printability and continuity.

2. Researching non-planar printing path generation methods to achieve path smoothness and material  uniformity.

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

**Why Robotics:**

This project necessitates the use of an industrial robot due to the intricate geometric features and functional  requirements of the artificial reef. The six-axis robotic arm enables continuous adjustment of the print head  orientation, allowing for the creation of complex surface textures and micro-topographies that are essential  for coral propagation. These capabilities are beyond the reach of conventional three-axis 3D printing or  manual fabrication methods, which cannot achieve the same degree of curvature control, material continuity,

or structural customization.

**2. Related Works**

**Project 1:**

"Fluid Forms" by Digital Building Technologies, ETH Zurich

This project developed an innovative robotic non-planar 3D printing method focused on decomposing  complex curved surfaces into printable structural segments. The research team used computational  algorithms to generate continuous printing paths aligned with principal stress directions, optimizing both  structural performance and material efficiency. Their breakthroughs in surface segmentation, structural line  extraction, and trajectory planning provide critical insights for our research on coral reef surface design and  printing strategy.

Source: https://dbt.arch.ethz.ch/project/fluid-forms/

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

![Image](data:image/png;base64,)

**Project 2:**

MX3D pioneered a large-scale robotic additive manufacturing system to construct a fully 3D-printed  stainless steel bridge in Amsterdam. The project employed multiple industrial robots working  collaboratively through wire arc additive manufacturing (WAAM) to fabricate free-form metal structures  at an architectural scale. Their experience in segmenting large structures, coordinating multi-robot printing  paths, and ensuring real-time quality control offers valuable engineering knowledge for our study.

Source: https://www.arup.com/projects/mx3d-bridge/
